see: PageUp and PageDown move one row fewer than a textarea (29 rows where Chrome pages 30 at 778 px), so the caret lands on a different row after a page key.
A PageDown that lands where a line wraps leaves the caret drawn at the end of the upper row instead of the start of the lower row, so Home, End, Up, Down and the next PageUp start from the wrong row.
PageUp or PageDown that reaches the first or last row stops on that row at the caret column instead of going on to the start or end of the text, as a textarea does.

Backspace or Delete that empties the caret piece, ends at a join or deletes on an empty line keeps the column Up and Down aim for, where a textarea forgets it, so the next Up or Down lands in another column.
In a browser where EditContext exists but making one throws, the browser notice does not show and the app fails to start the keyboard instead.
In Firefox or Safari the editor opens, takes no typing and draws a hollow cursor, with no notice that nullpad needs Chrome or Edge.

Up and Down aim from the caret boundary itself instead of the last whole pixel before it, so after wide glyphs such as an emoji the caret crosses the middle of the next glyph and lands after it where a textarea lands before it.
Fast wheel turns paint part or all of the screen blank for a frame or two, because Chrome scrolls on its compositor ahead of the lines the core draws.
An IME that converts letters already typed (reconversion, correction, accent for the letter before the caret) lands its conversion next to the letters it meant to replace, which stay on screen.
A fast wheel turn longer than one screen shows a blank band until the next frame, because only one screen of lines is drawn past each edge.
A 76-cell row of tabs or joined text nodes wraps one word early, where a textarea with the same text keeps it on the row.
The caret drawn after a join at trailing spaces sits one cell left, and a caret at a join where the line wraps is drawn at the end of the upper row instead of the start of the lower one.

Approximation: a Backspace from a caret drawn at the end of the upper row, which moves the caret to another row as the line rewraps, keeps the old goal x, so the next ArrowUp lands by the old x where a textarea aims at the caret x.
A character typed with AltGr on Windows (reported as Ctrl+Alt, such as @) is taken as a chord and cancelled, so it does not type.
Line numbers of five and six digits overflow the fixed-width gutter into the text.
Enter at a line start or at a join keeps a stale goal column, so the next Down after Up on the first line lands a column too far right.
Enter at a caret drawn at the end of the upper row (after Up onto a shorter row) keeps the goal, so the next Up lands at the end of the line instead of its start.
Enter inside a line forgets the goal cell Up and Down aim for, where a textarea keeps it, so the next Up or Down lands in another column.
